summary:
RedBeast is an open-source web app that lets anyone blink real NASA SPHEREx infrared images to see what changed in the sky. Pick one of five targets, or search any star name or sky coordinate, and the app cuts between real frames taken on different dates at matched wavelengths. Nothing is blended or animated, so whatever differs is in the data. Side-by-side, difference and 3D time-stack views show the same frames in other ways, and every frame carries its date, wavelength and quality flags.

Q-FIT, our robin assistant, is what makes it easy. Type "take me to the Sun", "go to Barnard" or "show the difference" in English or Turkish and Q-FIT does it on screen, then lets you pin the command as a shortcut. Navigation is rule-based, so it needs no language model and no API key. Q-FIT also cannot make things up: science answers arrive as source cards that cite the archive or paper behind them, and a candidate is never called a discovery.

The challenge asks for an easy way to see change over time in SPHEREx data. We tested ours on a known mover: across six frames, Barnard's Star shifts 2.04 pixels in 393 days, a 5.0σ detection that matches its catalogued motion. We say plainly that a Planet X would be too faint for a single frame.

SPHEREx data is public, but reading it takes a specialist. RedBeast gives classrooms and citizen scientists the same view.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

RedBeast is a blink comparator for real NASA SPHEREx images. Type a star name or a sky position (RA/Dec in degrees, hours or sexagesimal), or pick one of five ready targets, and the app shows real frames of that patch of sky taken on different dates. Moving objects shift between frames and variable objects change brightness. No account is needed, and the interface is in English and Turkish.

HOW IT WORKS

In SPHEREx every detector pixel sees a different wavelength, so the same star is observed at a different wavelength in almost every exposure. RedBeast only compares what is physically comparable:

- It queries the NASA/IPAC IRSA archive live and keeps the exposures whose wavelength at the target matches within half a bandwidth.

- It aligns frames using each file's own sky coordinates and never pins a source, so real motion survives.

- Bad pixels stay "no measurement" instead of black, and quality flags are read from each file's own header.

- Alignment is checked against Gaia DR3 stars in every sequence (0.4 to 1.3 arcsec on four of the five targets).

- When a new data release arrives, the newest reprocessing of each exposure is chosen automatically.

WAYS TO LOOK

- Blink with hard cuts between real frames, plus a filmstrip of every frame.

- Side by side, difference (B minus A), stack, and a co-moving stack that follows the star's catalogued motion.

- 3D time stack: frames lined up in depth by observation date, with the predicted track and the measured positions.

- Light curve, a spectrum built on the fly from all exposures, and Gaia DR3 and AllWISE catalogue overlays.

- Marks you can place on a frame and share with a read-only link that always reopens the same sequence.

- Field of view from 2 to 30 arcminutes.

BEYOND THE FRAMES

- Sky: an illustrated Milky Way with a "you are here" marker that flies down to the solar neighbourhood: 120 nearby Gaia DR3 stars, the five targets and 8,785 Hipparcos background stars. A year ruler from 2000 to 2100 moves them by their catalogued motion.

- Star: three clearly separate views. A 3D star built from catalogue radius and temperature, published evolution tracks (MIST, BHAC15, ATMO 2020), and an illustrative education model from 0.1 to 100 solar masses that ends in a white dwarf, a neutron star or a black hole.

MEET Q-FIT

Q-FIT is the robin in the corner, and it is the part we are proudest of. It is not a chatbot bolted onto the side: it drives the app. Type "take me to the Sun", "go to Barnard", "show the difference" or "go to the year 2080", in English or Turkish, and it does it on screen, then lets you pin the command as a shortcut. This navigation is rule-based, so it needs no language model and no API key. Q-FIT also cannot make things up: science answers come as source cards that cite the archive or paper behind them, the optional language model is off by default and must ask before it acts, and a candidate is never called a discovery.

WHAT WE FOUND WITH REAL DATA

- Barnard's Star: 6 frames over 393 days, moved 2.04 pixels (5.0σ), consistent with the catalogue.

- Epsilon Indi B: 6 frames over 525 days, moved 1.15 pixels (7.0σ), consistent with the catalogue.

- RW Aurigae: brightness changed 2.6 times over 371 days (5.6σ) while comparison stars stayed steady.

- WISE 0855−0714: not detected in a single frame, and reported as such.

- R Draconis: saturated in all 8 frames, so the app reports that brightness cannot be measured rather than inventing a light curve.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

SPHEREx data is public, but it arrives as specialist FITS files. RedBeast puts the same data in front of classrooms, citizen scientists and outreach audiences, and shows them honestly what SPHEREx can and cannot see. A Planet X would be too faint for a single frame, and we say so.

TOOLS

- Data: SPHEREx Level-2 spectral images (NASA/JPL-Caltech, served by IRSA), Gaia DR3, Hipparcos, AllWISE, SIMBAD.

- Backend: Python, FastAPI, Astropy, reproject, photutils, NumPy, SciPy, SQLite, with a documented OpenAPI interface.

- Frontend: TypeScript, React, three.js, GSAP, Vite.

- Quality: 400+ automated tests, Docker packaging, open source under the MIT licence. No special hardware: it runs on a laptop.

- AI use: coding assistants (OpenAI Codex, Claude) helped write and review the code. The idea, the data choices and the science checks are the team's.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE
